title: bin/lib/ — six primitives, fourteen implementations, no shared module
from: MEASURED, so this is a defect class and not tidiness. Six primitives, fourteen implementations: write_atomic in perry-conform + perry-decide + perry-migrate; load_schema in perry-decide + perry-conform + perry-task; resolve_state_root in perry-diagnose + viewer/parsers.py; project_lock and mint_id each in perry-decide + perry-task; heading_re in perry-lint + perry-task. EVERY REVIEW ROUND THIS SESSION FOUND AN INSTANCE OF EXACTLY THIS. squash versus .strip().lower() across bin/ and viewer/ (TASK-050, still open, silently loses a user's live risks). The writer's is-this-a-risk-table predicate being a second copy of the reader's. split_stages in two files. norm being squash under another name. Each was fixed one at a time; the structure that generates them was not touched. There is no shared module, so a second implementation is the path of least resistance every time. THE PATH HACK IS THE OTHER HALF. Eight sys.path.insert calls: seven tools reverse-import from viewer/, and three of them re-insert bin/ to import each other. viewer/parsers.py is 2,520 lines — the second-largest file in the repo — and it is the read side of every CLI tool while living in a directory named for the web viewer. tests/ imports it the same way. Whether it moves out of viewer/ or viewer/ stops being the anchor is the decision to make and state. THE GATE: behaviour-neutral. The suite is the proof and no test may need editing — that is what made the viewer/tables.py extraction safe, and it is the property to reproduce. from: viewer/parsers.py normalizes header cells with .strip().lower() at 11 sites; bin/perry-task and bin/perry-lint use squash, which also strips backticks and asterisks. On a header whose Risk cell is bolded, the writer says risk-table and the reader says not — so risk-add writes, perry-state reports 0 risks, perry-lint is clean and risk-migrate says already migrated. Four exits, all closed. Task tables survive only via positional fallbacks. to: SECOND-ROUND FIX 2026-08-18, after the V4 review FAILED this on the CATEGORY. The first pass unified viewer/parsers.py and reported done; the reviewer found THREE surviving second implementations in files that never imported squash — bin/perry-state twice (the Tracks header and the pack glossary header) and bin/perry-diagnose once (md_table, which reads the USER's board and OKR). from: BLOCKING FINDING FIXED 2026-08-18. The V4 re-review scored all five guarantees and found ADR-004 DOES NOT REOPEN — dry run complete and byte-identical to a cold apply, 0 ids and 0 characters lost across 30 files (mutation-tested: patching edit.after to drop a line made all 30 refuse with 0 bytes on disk), restore returns every file byte-identical, one declaration record via perry-conform, and partial migration behaves as designed. The one blocker was guarantee 3's failure path: only a write that LANDED WRONG was handled, so a write that FAILS — read-only file, full disk, permission revoked mid-run — propagated as an unhandled traceback, leaving a stranger's project N-of-M migrated with the restore point on disk and NEVER NAMED, the declaration never run, and empty stdout. A traceback names nothing. FIXED: the write is caught, the run is rolled back, and rollback_message names the restore point path and the exact recover command. THE PART THAT MATTERED MOST: undo() writes too, so the failure that broke the run can break the repair — the path is therefore named FIRST and unconditionally, and whether the automatic rollback succeeded is reported as a separate fact, so the worst case is not the one case that tells the user nothing. Also fixed: apply on a project with nothing writable raised KeyError 'run' in the renderer. 4 mutations red. gimegime-pmo 59 to 15 unchanged. AWAITING a fresh V4 on the fix.
to: V4 ROUND 3: FAIL on guarantee 3, ADR-004 STANDS — fixed 2026-08-18. The reviewer stopped guessing where the third crash was and ENUMERATED ALL FIVE PLACES MIGRATION WRITES TO A PROJECT. Rounds 1 and 2 had guarded two; three were unguarded, including the recovery path itself: do_restore's undo restored BOARD.md and then died unlinking conformance.md, leaving it half restored with the record still claiming conformance for a rolled-back file — the exact thing restore_point's own docstring exists to prevent. C.declare sat outside round 1's try, so a project migrated once and then locked down was FULLY migrated with the restore point on disk and never named. restore_point itself was unguarded. THE AXIS ALL THREE ROUNDS MISSED: a read-only DIRECTORY, not a read-only file — write_atomic renames, and a rename needs write permission on the directory, which is why every existing test, all driving read-only through a file, passed throughout. FIXED all three plus the scratch write in Linter.errors, guarded rather than exempted because an exemption list is where this kind of guard rots. AND THE ENUMERATION IS NOW A STANDING CHECK: tests/test_migrate.py TestEveryWriteSiteIsGuarded walks the AST and fails if any write call sits outside a try — proved by planting a sixth site after the guard was written and watching it go red. That is the fix; the three patches are not. Guarantees 1, 2, 4, 5 all PASS on gimegime-pmo (365 to 380 ids, none lost, 59 to 15, 30 declared, PolyForge refused in one sentence). TASK-079 affects guarantee 4 and not 3 — restore puts the read-only file's bytes back exactly; what the preview never mentions is the mode it is about to override. AWAITING a fresh V4.

from: SECOND-ROUND FIX 2026-08-18, after the V4 review FAILED this on the CATEGORY. The first pass unified viewer/parsers.py and reported done; the reviewer found THREE surviving second implementations in files that never imported squash — bin/perry-state twice (the Tracks header and the pack glossary header) and bin/perry-diagnose once (md_table, which reads the USER's board and OKR). Writing the category-shaped guard then found a FOURTH nobody had named: bin/perry-explain resolved headers with strip_md(c).lower(), a rule that differs from squash on internal whitespace — AND split rows with m.group(1).split('|'), a fifth splitter that does not honour the escape. Neither was reachable by TASK-050's or TASK-067's guards because BOTH were written against a hardcoded file list that did not name that file. THE DIVERGENCE IS REAL, not theoretical: '**Default** rung' lowers to 'default** rung' and matches nothing, so a project that bolded half a header lost the column silently and every track reported no default rung. Fixed at all four sites, header-only — the value normalizers (Status, Outcome, parse_frequency) keep their own rules deliberately, because they normalize what a project WROTE rather than which column it wrote it in, and widening the guard to cover them flags eight correct call sites. tests/test_one_header_rule.py holds the category: no reader builds a lowercased list over a row's cells, every table reader reaches squash, and perry-lint's norm alias is asserted to BE squash so it cannot quietly become a fifth copy. 4/4 mutations red. Suite 1075 to 1081. AWAITING a fresh V4.
to: V4 ROUND 3: FAIL. The decisive test the spec demanded — plant a new reader — came back GREEN, which IS the finding. The reviewer planted two plausible readers at HEAD, each resolving a header with strip-backtick-lower and carrying its own splitter: TASK-050's guard green, the decoration guard green, only TASK-067's guard red and only on the SPLITTER, never on the header rule. Three isolated blind spots, each measured separately: (1) SUBDIRECTORY — the byte-identical file is green at bin/lib/rows.py and red at bin/perry-rows-probe, because READERS uses iterdir plus is_file; this is the exact defect that had JUST been fixed in the sibling guard, unfixed one file over, and bin/lib is the directory TASK-065 exists to create. (2) SPELLING NOT SHAPE — 'for c in cells' red, 'for h in header' green; one variable rename walks past. (3) viewer/ is still a hardcoded one-file list, and the complement test skips any file lacking split_row, which exempts exactly the own-splitter-plus-own-header-rule combination that bit in perry-explain. AND A FIFTH LIVE COPY, found by AST over all 111 lowercasing sites: viewer/parsers.py read_conformance stripped backticks and spaces and LEFT ASTERISKS, so a bolded File header was read as a declaration and perry-conform status reported unreadable row against a correct file while perry-lint said clean. WHY FOUR COPIES SURVIVED THREE ROUNDS: the behavioural guard's fixture bolds WHOLE CELLS, and on whole-cell decoration the two rules AGREE — so exactly one guard can see the rule that shipped, and it is the one a new reader walks past. FIXED 2026-08-18: the fifth copy now uses squash, with plain/bolded/quoted/padded headers asserted identical, mutation red. STILL OPEN: all three guard blind spots.

from: DEFINITION CHANGED 2026-08-18 by ADR-006 (decide lane, user-decided). THIS ROW NO LONGER BUILDS WHAT ITS TITLE SAYS. DESIGN-005 section 6 step 4 now reads: the TASK STORE becomes canonical (perry/tasks.jsonl), BOARD.md becomes a projection, and the event log STAYS A LOG. Previously it read 'the event log becomes canonical', which fused two things section 4 never fused — decision #1 chose a structured store for tasks, decision #2 chose JSONL, and neither said the store and the log are one file. Section 5.2 did, on the stated ground of keeping ADR-002 satisfied, and ADR-002 is 'no cross-project registry' with no clause against a file inside a project and an explicit exemption for .perry/events.jsonl. The only reason given for one file was a citation that does not say what it was cited for. MEASURED BEFORE DECIDING: every full-set read is O(events) — 173 events for 75 tasks, a ratio that only rises — and 57 percent of the log's bytes are next events, cell overwrites with no replay value, in the file that must be traversed to answer section 1.3's own question. THREE LAYERS TO BUILD: perry/tasks.jsonl as truth (one object per task, current state, rewritten in place, under the STATE ROOT not .perry/ — location is the claim); BOARD.md as the rendered open subset; .perry/events.jsonl as history, append-only and disposable AGAIN. Still P1, still V5, still last of the four steps — the sequencing did not move, only what gets built. perry-task/list keeps its shape: where a value is read from is not a contract fact.

to: NARROWED BY ADR-007 2026-08-19, after its round-4 FAIL. The header rule dies for BOARD.md, OKR.md and .perry/config.md when TASK-094 deletes it — those files stop being tables. What REMAINS in this row's scope is design/*.md and .perry/roles/*.md, and under ADR-007 rule 2 Python stops parsing those entirely rather than resolving their headers correctly. So the four rounds of guard-versus-reviewer on this row are not worth a fifth: the category is being removed, not hardened. from: ALL ROUND 3 FINDINGS FIXED 2026-08-18, awaiting a fresh V4. Both decisive tests already passed in round 3 — a planted f-string writer and a planted raw-splitter reader were BOTH caught, and a hand-destroyed row reports ragged-row where it used to report clean. Criterion 1's two gaps are now closed: append_cell collapsed a line break at rc 0 where check_cell two functions above raises, and double-escaped a pipe on its re-render branch so the same value stored two ways depending on whether the row ended in a pipe — both halves now route through check_cell, four tests, two mutations red; and the refusals in perry-task and perry-goals printed the character but never the FIELD, so --next and --title gave identical messages — the offending value is now matched back to the argument that carried it, exact match only, because naming the wrong flag is worse than naming none. THE GUARD'S OWN BLIND SPOT, which the reviewer said it would flag hardest: _tools() used iterdir plus is_file and a non-recursive glob, so NO SUBDIRECTORY WAS VISIBLE and nine planted files stayed green, including bin/lib/rows.py — the directory TASK-065 exists to create. It walks the tree now, and HAND_ROW_RE matches an interpolation anywhere in the row rather than only in the first cell. AND ragged-row reported the SECTION HEADING's line rather than the row's: tables_with_lines is now the real scanner and tables() a view of it, verified with two ragged rows at known different lines because one sample cannot tell a constant offset from a coincidence — my first fix matched rows back by id() across two calls that build different objects and changed nothing, and my second was off by one. OUT OF SCOPE, as the reviewer recorded: the WHY/catalog entry, since the repo's catalog convention covers perry-diagnose ids only and that clause of criterion 5 is ambiguous.
to: NARROWED BY ADR-007 2026-08-19, after its round-4 FAIL. Once the three stores land, no markdown cell holds a value — so a writer cannot destroy a table it no longer writes, and a reader cannot mis-split a row that is not a row. The static guard that four rounds could not make category-shaped stops needing to be category-shaped. WHAT SURVIVES: adoption of a foreign project, which parses by definition, and that is where this row's remaining scope goes. The behavioural backstop (tests/test_escaped_pipe_corpus.py) survives too and is the right shape for it. KEEP OPEN until TASK-094/095 land.

title: perry-goals writer
from: ALL FIVE ROUND 3 FINDINGS FIXED 2026-08-18, awaiting a fresh V4. (1) The central one: render_row and check_cell were TWO guards while the docstring said one — splitlines splits on eleven boundaries and the membership test on two, so six characters were refused on create and accepted on amend. line_break_at() is now the single rule and a test forbids either caller from spelling the test itself; the six are enumerated FROM THE LANGUAGE, not from the bug report, which named two. (2) Refused was raised in viewer/tables.py and defined nowhere in it, reachable through --close/--miss on a Commitments table with no Status column, giving a NameError where a refusal belongs; it now raises this module's own exception. (3) A refusal names the FLAG — index is a column position and means nothing to the person who typed the command, so --next and --title gave identical messages; the offending value is matched back to the argument that carried it, exact match only. (4) Whitespace-only was refused on create and ERASED the cell on amend, because that branch tested is-not-None where the other strips; --discharged-by is deliberately excluded and a test pins that exclusion. (5) append_separator_cell assumed a trailing pipe where append_cell handles its absence, so a widen produced a 7-cell header against a 6-cell separator at rc 0 with lint silent. Every fix mutation-verified. TWO OF MY OWN TESTS WERE FAKE AND MUTATIONS CAUGHT BOTH: one asserted the whitespace guard's source construct existed and stayed green when the condition inside it became if-False, rewritten at CLI level against the file; one sliced 900 bytes of source and asserted against the window, which found the wrong region and went red on correct code.
to: NARROWED BY ADR-007 2026-08-19. perry-goals' writer moves to a store under TASK-092, so its open findings about cell escaping and the create/amend split stop applying to OKR.md — a JSON string carries a line break without a guard. WHAT STILL APPLIES: the flag-naming in refusals, and the module-scope handler class of bug, neither of which is about markdown. Re-scope when TASK-092 lands.

title: Split perry-task by subcommand group
from: NOW BLOCKED ON TASK-038 AS WELL AS TASK-065, and the reason is not the line count. MEASURED at 34bd472: class Board is 446 lines of perry-task's 3,291 (13.6 percent); the write side TASK-038 deletes — ensure_columns, ensure_section, ensure_section_columns, append_row, append_section_row, replace_row, remove_row, last_row — is 152 lines, 4.6 percent. The read side, 273 lines, STAYS, because KR-O2.2 requires a hand edit to raise a reconcile prompt rather than be overwritten, and detecting a hand edit means reading the board. So the audit's 'the write-side half of 531 plus 437 lines' overstates it: 152 lines alone would NOT justify blocking this row. THE REAL OVERLAP IS STRUCTURAL. This row's own gate says the three-way atomic write (board row + journal line + event) and the single project lock must stay single, and that a split giving two files their own commit path is worse than the file being long. After TASK-038 there IS no three-way write — one append, one render. Splitting 22 subcommands around an invariant that is about to be replaced means the split's one hard decision gets made twice. That is this row's own argument about TASK-065, one level up, applied to itself.
to: RECONSIDER UNDER ADR-007 2026-08-19. Splitting perry-task by subcommand group was sized against a tool that parses and writes markdown. Under ADR-007 that tool loses its board reader, its row renderer and its cell escaping — TASK-090, 094 and 095 between them. The split may be unnecessary at the smaller size, or may want different seams. Do not start this before TASK-095; sizing a refactor against code that is about to be deleted is how a refactor becomes wasted.

title: perry-task: Top risks becomes a table with id / opened / cleared
from: RE-REVIEWED 2026-08-18, and the root cause was WORSE than reported: FOUR implementations of 'where is this section', not three, giving three different answers in one call. On a board whose heading reads ## **Top risks** — a human bolding a heading, which no rule forbids — parse_board saw no section (0 risks), ensure_section saw none either so risk-add APPENDED A SECOND ## Top risks at exit 0, and the id minter read the rows by a third rule and numbered from them. Every risk already recorded became invisible to every tool and perry-lint said nothing. FIXED: one predicate, viewer/parsers.py heading_is, decoration-tolerant via the same squash the header cells use; bin/perry-task gains heading_matches sharing it; ensure_section and named_section and has_section route through it. THE FOURTH was found by fixing the other three and re-running — top_risks_section had a regex of its own, so the reader still reported zero after the writer was fixed. Verified end to end on the bolded shape: 0 to 2 risks seen before the write, one section after it, 3 risks after, and risk-clear can address the earlier ids again. tests/test_one_heading_predicate.py asserts all four agree across 7 decorated spellings including Chinese, and keeps the boundary the old regex protected (## P2 must not match ## P20). 4 mutations red; a fifth came back green because it undid only one of the two places the fix touched, and was redone against the predicate itself. AWAITING a fresh V4.

from: FOUND 2026-08-18 while fixing TASK-044's planning crash, by asserting what I ASSUMED rather than what happens — the test failed and the code was right. write_atomic writes a .tmp and calls Path.replace, and A RENAME NEEDS WRITE PERMISSION ON THE DIRECTORY, NOT ON THE TARGET. So a file the user has chmod-ed read-only is migrated like any other, and nothing in the plan says the bit was there. THE QUESTION IS A POLICY ONE ABOUT SOMEBODY ELSE'S FILES and I deliberately did not decide it mid-fix: (a) the bit is an explicit user signal and ADR-004's whole posture is 'the user declares', so migration should refuse or at least name it; (b) it may be incidental — copied off a read-only medium, or a stale mode from an archive — and refusing would block a migration for a reason unrelated to shape. PINNED BY A TEST TODAY: the file IS migrated, and the restore point carries its original bytes, so the recovery path covers it — which is what makes the current behaviour survivable rather than merely undetected. NOT TRUE TODAY: that the plan mentions the mode at all. Whichever way this is decided, TASK-044-spec says migration is 'not silent — every file it touched, listed, with what changed in each', and a permission it overrode belongs in that list.

reason: The measurement this row asked for was made (TASK-110) and it argues against the row. The whole proposal recovers 560,089 bytes — 1.4 days of growth at the measured 405,349 bytes/day — once, and nothing in it keeps pace. The cost is also not paid where the bytes are: perry-lint reads all 135 evidence files in 8ms and no agent loads evidence/ per turn. Rule B's selector decays; rule A deletes the argument history a project that reviews this hard depends on. The lever the measurement does point at is how much prose a V4 round emits, which is a product decision, not this row. Dropped on the evidence, not for lack of interest.

title: When migration encounters a file the user has chmod-ed read-only, should it refuse to touch that file, or migrate it and name the overridden permission in the plan? Today it migrates silently: write_atomic renames over the target, and a rename needs write permission on the directory, not on the file.
answer: Migrate and name the override; do not refuse. Reasoning recorded because the row was minted for it: refusing would block a whole migration for a reason unrelated to shape, and migration is the one road ADR-004 gives an undeclared project — a refusal there is the wall with no door that this project rejects everywhere else. The override is also reversible: the restore point carries the file's original bytes, verified under TASK-079. The 'at least name it' half of the ADR-004 posture is already satisfied by what shipped in PR #6, and TASK-115 added the guard that keeps that wording an observation rather than advice. The read-only bit stays a signal Perry reports and does not act on.

TASK-203 has now failed THREE V4 rounds, all three mine, and every one has ended with the same defect: an ordinary command silently truncates a canonical register store. I said I would escalate rather than attempt a fourth, so here it is. ROUND 3's FAIL: the gate is read at a moment the command controls. cmd_add's queue-mode branch calls ensure_section('Intake') BEFORE commit() asks the gate, so the gate sees a freshly created, readable, EMPTY table, answers yes, derives [] and writes zero bytes. Measured: a 291-byte 3-record intake.jsonl goes to 0 on 'perry-task add --track ops' with rc 0, byte-identical on 45a355d, and perry-lint reports '0 row(s) drifted'. It is round 1's blocking finding word for word — round 2 closed it for the project-mode track and never asked the queue-mode track, which is the mode ## Intake exists for. Three more doors of the same shape: intake 3->1, ask 3->1, risk-add 3->1, all rc 0, all preserved on base. THE DECISION. (A) Evaluate the gate against the board AS IT WAS AT COMMAND ENTRY, not after the command mutated it — snapshot the shape before any board write. Principled and small, but it is the fourth 'move the question' fix on this row and the first three all looked principled too. (B) RECOMMENDED — make it structurally impossible: an ordinary write may never SHRINK a canonical store. Only an explicit removal command (purge, resolve-intake, intake-sweep) may reduce the record count, and any derivation that would produce fewer records than the store holds is a refusal, not a write. That is one invariant covering every door found in three rounds — the command name, the non-unique tuple, the four section shapes, and the ensure_section ordering — instead of a fourth predicate. (C) Revert TASK-203 entirely and reconsider the row. It has introduced a store-truncation regression in all three rounds; before it, intake.jsonl did not exist and could not be wrong. That is a real 'should we do this at all' question and it deserves an answer, not an assumption. (D) Narrow the scope to the risks register only, which is the one that already existed, and defer intake/asks. NOTE THIS AFFECTS THE PHASE: TASK-203 is the ONLY row under P003-O1-KR1, and DoD Must-Have 2 names intake.jsonl and asks.jsonl explicitly, so (C) or (D) means the phase misses that Must-Have deliberately rather than by accident. title: perry-decide REISSUES a retired ADR id, and perry-task does not — two tools, one contract, opposite answers. Measured by the TASK-235 agent 2026-08-29: delete ADR-011's file and the next mint hands out 011 again. perry-task purge retires an id through the append-only event log so it is never reissued; perry-decide writes NO events at all, so it has nothing to retire an id with. Worse, before TASK-235 the behaviour was NON-DETERMINISTIC: on main an unrelated write re-rendered the index and the next mint reissued anyway. THE STAKE: an ADR id is an address. ADR-007 is cited by name in ADR-010, in DESIGN-013, in three task rows and in this project's own commit messages. If 011 can name two different decisions, every one of those citations becomes ambiguous the moment an ADR is deleted and a new one minted. This did not matter while nobody deleted ADRs; TASK-235 is the row that made deletion ordinary. THE OPTIONS. (a) RECOMMENDED — perry-decide writes events like every other writer, and an id is retired the way perry-task retires one. This is the answer that makes the two tools agree rather than documenting why they differ, and DESIGN-004's whole posture is that every write goes through a tool and leaves a trace. Cost: perry-decide gains an event surface it does not have today. (b) Refuse the delete instead: an ADR file may not be removed, only superseded — which is arguably what a decision record SHOULD mean, since ADR-005 and ADR-007 are cited as history and history is not deleted. Cheaper, and it may be more correct in principle. (c) Accept reissue, and document that an ADR id is a slot rather than an address. Honest but it silently breaks every existing citation. (d) Leave it declared as it is now — the TASK-235 agent pinned the disagreement with a named test rather than resolving it silently, so nothing is hidden and the row can close. My recommendation is (b) THEN (a): stop the deletion that creates the problem, then give perry-decide the event surface so the two tools stop disagreeing on principle rather than by accident. But (b) changes what a decision record IS, which is yours and not mine.

summary: The two paragraphs TASK-243 wrote as its section 7 and which its V4 reviewer said should be rows rather than prose. FIRST, the fourth ending TASK-243 considered and rejected: 'a register write must not honour rows it did not address'. It was rejected because intake is position-keyed so the blast radius is real, and the reviewer accepted that rejection — but rejecting an ending inside one row is not the same as deciding the question, and today an ordinary write still carries every board row forward including ones the command never looked at. SECOND, the literal property TASK-243's own spec named and could not deliver: 'the drift report must not decrease while canonical records are being destroyed'. Its close was ruled acceptable, on the reasoning that the literal wording would require lint to report a disagreement that no longer exists and that the defect filed was the SILENCE, which is closed. What is still missing is a durable 'somebody has seen this' surface with a clearing condition — a place where a destruction stays visible after the write that announced it has scrolled away.

title: tests/run's output offers THREE numbers that all look like a failure count, and two of the three are wrong
from: Measured on this repository 2026-08-30, and it has already misled two agents. Grepping '^FAIL:' gives 3; summing the per-module 'FAILED (failures=N)' gives 4; and the summary line reads 'N module(s) red', which is 3. Only the sum is the failure count. The cause: tests/run prints test_diagnose's test_the_queue_register_reconciles_with_the_queue_on_this_repository as a BARE TRACEBACK with no FAIL: prefix, while the other three carry it. THE IRONY IS THE FINDING: TASK-239's author disclosed this exact trap about its OWN harness in its result — 'named_failures collects lines prefixed FAIL: / ERROR:, and tests/run prints one of the pre-existing failures as a bare traceback with no such prefix' — found it, said it out loud, and corrected for it by reporting deltas rather than absolute counts. It is the same trap that then produced the number that author was second-guessed on. Its reviewer walked into it too, on the first grep of its own log, and only caught it because it went looking for why another agent's number differed. The whole baseline dispute of 2026-08-30 — 4 versus 3 at the same commit — was this, not board state and not uncommitted edits.
to: MECHANISM FOUND 2026-08-30 by the TASK-249 agent while retracting a number this trap had produced: tests/parallel:283 prints a red module's stderr TRUNCATED TO ITS LAST 25 LINES, and nothing is visibly elided. test_diagnose fails twice; the second failure's FAIL: header survives that window and the FIRST ONE'S DOES NOT, so the first arrives as a bare traceback with no prefix. That is why the output offers three numbers that all look like a failure count — grepping ^FAIL: gives 3, summing the per-module FAILED (failures=N) gives 4, and the summary line 'N module(s) red' gives 3 — and only the sum is right. It has now caught three agents in twelve hours, one of whom had DOCUMENTED the trap in its own result before walking into it, and one of whom used it to accuse a correct measurement of being wrong. The truncation is the root cause: the missing prefix is not a formatting choice, it is a line that fell off the top of a 25-line window.

title: A signed-off test pins a line number by hand and it moved twice in one row (adoption-suppression, 374 -> 402): raised by the TASK-239 agent against its own work. title: .perry/conformance.md is a pure ledger with a hand-rolled table parser, and its phantom row has nowhere to record provenance
from: Measured 2026-08-29 at a30e103. The file is 38 lines: a 10-line prose header that is ALREADY a constant in the writer (bin/perry-conform:406 HEADER) and 24 rows of four regular columns — File, Shape version, Declared, Route — with not one word of per-row prose. render() at bin/perry-conform:423 rebuilds the whole file from the declarations on every write_atomic, so unlike .perry/config.md this one already round-trips from its own records. title: bash tests/run WRITES PERRY STATE INTO THE REPOSITORY IT RUNS IN — four files, via an intake-sweep discharging a real board row
from: Proved by a controlled experiment by the TASK-050 round 11 agent, 2026-08-30, and independently the cause of a stray event the PMO caught in TASK-241's merge an hour earlier. Running the suite modifies .perry/events.jsonl, perry/BOARD.md, perry/intake.jsonl and perry/journal/<today>.md in whatever repository it executes in, by running an intake-sweep that discharges one board row. The experiment: restore the four files, run the suite, and the same four move again. THE SWEEP IS IDEMPOTENT, WHICH IS WHY A SECOND RUN LOOKS CLEAN — that is why nobody noticed. It matters beyond tidiness: two of the suite's three standing failures are data-dependent on board state, so the suite perturbs the very state its own results depend on. It is also how a stray intake-sweep event with actor 'agent' ended up committed on a coding branch and was caught only because an append-only file conflicted at merge; a fast-forward would have carried it into main silently.
to: V4 ROUND 2: PASS with three defects, one blocking merge. Review at review/task-249-round2 a8de48c. All four attacked claims held: the refuse-to-start guard runs green with PERRY_PROJECT unset and with ==ROOT, rc=2 on a foreign value, refuses before step 1, names both paths and prints the escape command — and the companion test dies alone against the PLAUSIBLE wrong version ('if [ -n $PERRY_PROJECT ]'), which is the version that would actually have been written. The four IGNORE_DIRS deletions really do match nothing (zero hits tracked, on disk, in CI, in .vscode). 'By consequence' is load-bearing: with each equality pin ALSO deleted, the planting test still kills all three blindings, and for IGNORE_NAMES it dies alone. 12 fresh mutations, 12/12 red. The retraction is complete — no surviving assertion of '3' or of the accusation anywhere in code, docs or commit messages. DEFECT 1 (blocks merge): tests/tree_guard.py:60-67 still says tests/run 'closes the ambient case by exporting PERRY_PROJECT=ROOT for the whole run'. It REFUSES instead; the export was tried and rejected. A withdrawn approach described as shipped, inside the one list whose job is to tell the reader what the guard does NOT catch. DEFECT 2: 'eleven executables' at tree_guard.py:129 and test_tree_guard.py:348 is declared and wrong — measured 24, of which 18 under bin/. The result document dropped the number; the code did not. DEFECT 3: the refusal compares raw strings against 'pwd -P' while perry-task .resolve()s, so a /tmp symlink alias of ROOT and a trailing slash both refuse a harmless environment — and the guard's own test passes root.resolve(), the one spelling that cannot trip it. ALSO: .claude/worktrees/ and .gstack/ exist, are tool-written, and are named in neither ignore list; and the deletion of the four names contradicts the same docstring's .git rationale nine lines above, so a cache dir appearing mid-run now reads '+ .ruff_cache' red (fails safe, so not a blocker).

title: Two V4 reviewers measured the SAME commit within an hour and got different failure counts (4/3 and 5/4 at main@5367c06); the difference is the recorded test_host_support flake, but nothing in the suite output says so. A reviewer who measures 5 has no way to tell a flake from a regression except by asking another reviewer, and the second measurement is exactly what a review is supposed to make unnecessary. Either the flake is quarantined and named in the output, or the suite prints its own known-flaky set so a count that includes one is legible as such. Related: TASK-251 (three numbers that all look like a failure count).

The PMO handed a wrong baseline to a review brief: I wrote '4 failures across 2 red modules' when it is 3, and omitted the test_host_support flake that makes a first run on a fresh worktree read 5/4. The TASK-249 reviewer caught and corrected it. This is the same defect the project just wrote a knowledge card about (verification/numbers-migrate-between-sentences) committed by the person who wrote the card, in a brief sent an hour later. Filed against the PMO. The fix is not more care: review briefs should carry the command that produces the baseline instead of the baseline, so the reviewer measures rather than trusts.

title: The tree guard cannot see a new top-level DIRECTORY it ignores by name, and one such hole is now taken knowingly: measured on TASK-249 round 3, with .claude/, .gstack/ and .ruff_cache/ all appearing between snapshot and verify, only .ruff_cache is reported and '+ .claude' is not, because dirnames are filtered before directory entries are recorded. perry-decide REISSUES a retired ADR id, and perry-task does not — two tools, one contract, opposite answers. Measured by the TASK-235 agent 2026-08-29: delete ADR-011's file and the next mint hands out 011 again. perry-task purge retires an id through the append-only event log so it is never reissued; perry-decide writes NO events at all, so it has nothing to retire an id with. Worse, before TASK-235 the behaviour was NON-DETERMINISTIC: on main an unrelated write re-rendered the index and the next mint reissued anyway. THE STAKE: an ADR id is an address. ADR-007 is cited by name in ADR-010, in DESIGN-013, in three task rows and in this project's own commit messages. If 011 can name two different decisions, every one of those citations becomes ambiguous the moment an ADR is deleted and a new one minted. This did not matter while nobody deleted ADRs; TASK-235 is the row that made deletion ordinary. THE OPTIONS. (a) RECOMMENDED — perry-decide writes events like every other writer, and an id is retired the way perry-task retires one. This is the answer that makes the two tools agree rather than documenting why they differ, and DESIGN-004's whole posture is that every write goes through a tool and leaves a trace. Cost: perry-decide gains an event surface it does not have today. (b) Refuse the delete instead: an ADR file may not be removed, only superseded — which is arguably what a decision record SHOULD mean, since ADR-005 and ADR-007 are cited as history and history is not deleted. Cheaper, and it may be more correct in principle. (c) Accept reissue, and document that an ADR id is a slot rather than an address. Honest but it silently breaks every existing citation. (d) Leave it declared as it is now — the TASK-235 agent pinned the disagreement with a named test rather than resolving it silently, so nothing is hidden and the row can close. My recommendation is (b) THEN (a): stop the deletion that creates the problem, then give perry-decide the event surface so the two tools stop disagreeing on principle rather than by accident. But (b) changes what a decision record IS, which is yours and not mine.
answer: (a), scoped to a high-water mark. perry-decide appends a mint event to .perry/events.jsonl and mint_id takes max(files union events), so an id once issued is never reissued -- the same rule as perry-task's minting_records. Three measurements on d49964e reshaped the choice and belong to the implementing row. (1) Only the HIGHEST id reissues; a middle gap is never filled -- delete ADR-002 of five and the next mint is ADR-006 -- so what is needed is a durable high-water mark, not an event surface on every command. (2) Option (b) "refuse the delete" was rejected because perry-decide has no delete command to refuse: bootstrap/new/supersede/status/list only, and an ADR leaves decisions/ by a human rm, so (b) could only ever be documentation plus a lint detector, never enforcement. (3) The cheap counter-file fix is foreclosed by TASK-235's own guard, tests/test_decide_writer.py:461 ADR_ONLY = ^decisions/ADR-\d+-[^/]+\.md$, which permits nothing but ADR bodies in decisions/. The remaining durable home is .perry/events.jsonl, whose schema owner is "perry" rather than a lane, so decide writing there does not breach the hand-off contract. Current exposure: ADR-012 is the top id (8 citations); ADR-007 (321) and ADR-004 (237) are reachable only after every id above them is deleted first.

title: Should the adoption reader be fenced at all, now that it has no caller? P003-O2-KR2's metric asks for 'the adoption reader fenced into one named module, with a mechanical guard shown able to go red'. Its own re-baseline of 2026-09-01 then removed the ground under it: bin/perry-migrate was DELETED 2026-08-31 by TASK-261, TASK-097 was dropped with it, and /perry adopt is a user-facing command whose implementation went too. So viewer/parsers.py's 4,603 lines now serve ONE role, and the KR text says in its own words that 'whether an unreachable reader is still worth fencing is the open question TASK-099 carries into the pivot rather than an assumption this KR may keep making'. The phase file lists this under User Commitments as 'a product decision rather than a review'. THE OPTIONS. (a) FENCE IT ANYWAY -- a boundary that exists before the caller returns is cheaper than one retrofitted after, and /perry adopt is a documented command someone will re-implement. Cost: a guard around code nothing calls, which is also a guard nothing exercises, and an unexercised guard is the class of check this project keeps finding rotten. (b) DO NOT FENCE; delete the adoption half instead, on the ground that ADR-011 already condemns viewer/parsers.py as the representation layer and a reader with no caller is dead code by definition. Cost: /perry adopt cannot be re-implemented without restoring it, and the deletion is not this phase's declared scope. (c) FENCE ONLY WHAT THE STORE READERS TOUCH -- draw the boundary from the live side rather than the dead side, so the guard is exercised by code that actually runs. My recommendation, because it is the only one of the three whose guard can be shown able to go red by a test of live behaviour. (d) DEFER the whole KR to phase 004 and score P003-O2-KR2 as withdrawn, since its premise was deleted mid-phase. An unset actor is exactly why this incident cannot be closed by reading the log. Deliverable is that answer plus whatever it implies: either --actor becomes required on writing subcommands, or the event records enough about its invocation that a write can be traced without it. Do not spend the round hunting the original five events; they are the evidence, not the work.

title: Should the adoption reader be fenced at all, now that it has no caller? THE PREMISE WAS WRONG, and this is the finding rather than the decision: the KR asks for "the adoption reader fenced into ONE NAMED MODULE", and that module does not exist and never did. Measured on 185c208: viewer/parsers.py is 4,606 lines and EIGHT tools import it -- perry-task, perry-lint, perry-goals, perry-decide, perry-diagnose, perry-knowledge, perry_store.py, perry_md_store.py. So a consumer that can run the tool NEVER needs to parse the markdown, and one that reads the store alone would get it wrong on a store-less project -- the tool's fallback is the thing that makes both cases answer the same. tests/fixtures/sample-project reports state_root '' only because its own config.md declares no such line, not because the fallback is missing. THEREFORE the page should say: read state_root off the payload; .perry/config.jsonl is the register and .perry/config.md is its projection; the tool falls back to the projection when the register is absent, so a consumer never has to. aiMark declined to implement the markdown fallback for exactly this reason and asked whether any consumer must resolve the root itself. title: TASK-285 has FAILed two V4 rounds and perry-lint says another round is not the next step. UNUSUALLY, THE PRINCIPLE HAS ALREADY BEEN NAMED -- by the round 2 reviewer, not by me -- and I have already implemented it. This ask exists to have you confirm or overrule that, because a PMO who has just fixed something is the worst judge of whether the principle is settled. WHAT HAPPENED. The row writes one rule into three shipped files: a dispatched agent works in its own git worktree, the primary checkout is never switched by an agent and merges the branch afterwards. Round 1 defeated the guard by softening the rule to 'MAY ... where convenient' -- every assertion pinned the presence of words, none pinned modality. I fixed that with a denylist of eight hedge words. Round 2 then kept the pinned imperative VERBATIM, used none of the eight, and added one sentence inside the rule's own blockquote: 'Where a worktree is impractical, sharing the primary checkout instead is an acceptable alternative.' All nine tests reported OK with the headline deliverable retracted. It also walked past the push check with two synonyms (publishes / raises a pull request). Its summary: A DENYLIST OVER ENGLISH HAS NOW LOST THIS ARGUMENT TWICE. THE OPTIONS. (a) IMPLEMENTED AND MY RECOMMENDATION -- an allowlist. The rule block is compared literally and four normative regions are pinned by sha256; any addition, removal or rewording reddens. Rationale prose is deliberately NOT pinned, so the observed-failure account and the local-merge argument can still be improved without touching a test; what an agent is TOLD TO DO cannot change silently. Thirteen mutations, thirteen red, including both that defeated the old design and a single extra space. Cost: changing the rule now requires re-pinning a digest in the same commit, which is friction on purpose. This is the same move you chose in USER-904 (one header_index over a smarter detector) and USER-906 (one invariant over a fourth predicate). (b) Keep a denylist and widen it again. The record says this is the third widening and the first two each looked principled. (c) Accept the guard as advisory, close at a lower rung, document the limit. (d) Drop the guard entirely and rely on the fact that the rule is now in three files a reader sees. STATED LIMIT OF (a), because it is real: an allowlist pins what EXISTS and cannot cover a fifth normative region someone adds later in a file it does not read. Evidence: evidence/2026-09/TASK-285-round2-v4-review.md and TASK-285-result.md.

title: TASK-067 has FAILed two V4 rounds and needs a principle chosen, not a third round. THE CENSUS THAT MAKES THIS ANSWERABLE NOW EXISTS: TASK-323 delivered a bound and a census and PASSED V4 round 2 on 2026-09-03, so unlike the last two rounds this choice is against measured numbers rather than a recollection. Both failed rounds carried criteria-unbounded because the criteria file had no bound; it now has one -- 89 members (27 W1 / 18 W2 / 38 R1 / 6 R2), last element viewer/tables.py:280, generated by a runnable script at evidence/2026-09/TASK-323-bound.py. Census: 20 rows, 12 caught, 8 uncaught, plus 13 shape rows with 4 red controls. THE TWO READINGS, with what each would actually have to cover. (A) EVERY WRITE PATH MUST REFUSE AN UNRENDERABLE CELL. Population is all writers. To close it must cover all 27 W1 members, already refusing, PLUS the 7 uncaught separator-row builders -- perry-task:985, :1034, :1112, :5174, perry_md_store.py:774, perry-goals:327-328, perry-goals:3093 -- PLUS bin/perry-decide:332, which guards with a weaker third spelling that misses a trailing newline, PLUS perry-task:7431. It would NOT cover the five uncaught read shapes, which are not writes. Its cost is visible in the bound itself: the population has no last element other than the current line count, which is exactly why this file had no bound for two rounds and why each round found a member the previous one never reached. (B) ONE CHOKE POINT PLUS ONE DETECTOR, MY RECOMMENDATION. To close it must cover ONE SYMBOL -- nothing outside render_row builds a row -- with ragged-row as the backstop. The census says precisely what that buys and what it does not: it covers the 7 separator builders by construction IF separator rows are routed through the choke point too, which they are not today; its backstop is MEASURED to work on w4-w7 and MEASURED not to exist for r2/r3/r4/r7/r8; ragged-row cannot cover the read side at all and .split('|', 6) proves no count-based check ever will; its detector has four demonstrated blind spots on the read half because SPLIT_RE matches none of maxsplit, re.split, a SEP constant, or .rsplit/.partition; and it does not reach perry-decide:332, which builds no rows. TWO MORE FACTS THE ROUNDS DID NOT HAVE. First, ragged-row fires ONLY inside a table the schema recognises -- round 1 confirmed with a control that the identical 8-cell row is silent in an unrecognised section -- so on a project filing work under its own headings via add --group, which Perry explicitly supports, (B)'s backstop does not exist. Second, both readings leave perry-task:7431 open; it is a message-quality defect rather than a corruption path. PRECEDENT, OFFERED AS PRECEDENT AND NOT AS AN ARGUMENT: you chose shape (B) in USER-904 after seven rounds and USER-906 after three. The census neither confirms nor contradicts that -- (B)'s one-symbol surface is real and measured, and so is the fact that its detector is green on nine shapes, five of which have no backstop of any kind. Evidence: evidence/2026-08/TASK-067-finding.md sections Bound, Census and The two readings; evidence/2026-09/TASK-323-round2-v4-review.md.

to: bin/perry-task is to be split into one file per subcommand group. The split is deliberately left unsized for now: the markdown reader, the row renderer and the cell escaping are all on their way out of that file, and re-measuring once they are gone is cheaper than splitting it twice.

title: Agent is five strings that do not join, and role has never once been written
to: Perry represents an agent as five separate strings that never join into one record, and the `role` field has never once been written on any row. Who owns the agent register was settled on 2026-08-20 — work owns `.perry/agents.jsonl` and `.perry/roles/` — so what the row still needs is a spec before it can be dispatched.

title: four of six document collections are unreachable through any contract
to: Four of Perry's six document collections cannot be reached through any published contract. Deferred on 2026-08-21 by the user, with the cost recorded rather than waved through: aiMark reads those directories directly for now, which knowingly makes it a second reader of Perry's LAYOUT, so a consumer holding `perry/design/` breaks silently the first time a project moves its state root.

title: ## Cadence becomes a store
to: Perry keeps six registers as JSONL stores that tools read and write through. `BOARD.md § Cadence` is not one of them and is still a markdown table nothing owns. This row converts it.

title: Perry has no writer for a migration event, so TASK-180 hand-wrote JSON into an append-only log
to: Perry records every other kind of event through a writer that owns the event's shape. A migration event has no writer at all, so TASK-180 appended hand-written JSON straight into the append-only event log.

title: a write returns no seq, so a poll cannot tell a stale read from a fresh one
to: A Perry write returns no sequence number. So a consumer that polls has no way to tell whether what it just read already reflects its own write or predates it, and a stale read is indistinguishable from a fresh one.

title: no compare-and-set on a write, and the board demonstrably moves between a read and a write
to: Nothing lets a caller say 'write this only if the board is still what I read'. There is no compare-and-set on a Perry write, and the board demonstrably does move between a read and the write that follows it, so two writers can silently overwrite each other.

title: perry-diagnose asks 'is this ask answered' with a word search over free prose, and disagrees with the store in both directions
to: perry-diagnose answers 'has this ask been answered?' by searching for words in free prose rather than by reading the ask register. It disagrees with the store in both directions — reporting answered asks as pending and pending ones as answered.

title: an Objective is not a record, so it has no durable address
to: An Objective has no id, so nothing can point at one durably: `okr.objectives[].id` is empty for all five. The phase level already solved exactly this — `phase/002-linkage.md` states `id: O1` and the payload carries it — and the contract already accepts a STATED id where it refuses a derived one. DESIGN-009 was drafted for it on 2026-08-21 with four user decisions still open.

title: OKR setting is a ten-field checklist where it should be an elicitation
to: Setting an OKR is currently a ten-field checklist to be filled in, where it should be an elicitation that draws the answers out. DESIGN-011 was drafted for it on 2026-08-21 with four user decisions open. Its step 2 is the real gate: run the question bank against a project that has no OKR.md and score the output with the rubric, or the claim that the rubric surfaces zero issues is not measured at all.

title: DESIGN-006 F — a finance-shaped role runs one real task end to end
to: The first role card for work that is not software — a finance-shaped role, run end to end on one real task. All four dependencies are done, so it is startable; the real blocker is that every role card shipped so far is software-shaped, so this is the first honest test of whether the role model generalises. The run itself and its V5 signature stay with the user.

title: writing about an id costs a dangling entry, and three records tonight paid it
to: Writing about a task id in prose costs a dangling-reference entry, and three records did on one night. The row is to decide the rule for the five dangling ids that resulted — widen the report's mark beyond the paragraph, exempt evidence records wholesale, or accept the cost in writing — and then make the reconcile test assert whichever was chosen.

title: Nothing tells an agent a projection is behind its store — ADR-012's rule has no surface
to: ADR-012 decided that an agent should detect when a projection is behind the store it is derived from, and nothing in Perry surfaces that. This is the whole implementation of the detection half: a per-pair mtime comparison replacing about 3,100 lines of drift census. Perry's own history is the argument for building the surface rather than writing the instruction — an instruction with nothing behind it does not get run.

title: the tasks store is the only one of six whose census line does not name it: 'store: 225 record(s)' and 'drift against the store', where the other five say risks/OKR/config/intake/ask store
to: Perry reports six stores and names five of them. The tasks store alone prints `store: 225 record(s)` and `drift against the store`, where the other five say risks store, OKR store, config store, intake store and ask store — so the one line a reader is most likely to be looking at is the one that does not say what it is about.

title: viewer/parsers.py:3899-3900 builds top_risks from BOARD.md while perry/risks.jsonl exists, reached from perry-state:1631 — the task and OKR readers beside it already prefer their stores (TASK-095 V4 round 1, finding 4)
to: The top-risks reader still builds its answer from `BOARD.md` even though `perry/risks.jsonl` exists and is canonical. The task and OKR readers sitting next to it in the same file already prefer their stores, so this one reader is the odd one out rather than the norm.

title: test_risks_store's TestTheReadersAreOneFunction fails 3 assertIs identity checks under 'unittest discover' and passes under 'bash tests/run' and in isolation — a module-double-import artifact, independently observed by two reviewers on 2026-08-29; the suite's answer depends on the runner and nothing says so
to: A test module passes when run alone and fails three identity assertions when run under `unittest discover`, because of a module double-import artifact. Two reviewers observed it independently on 2026-08-29. The defect worth fixing is not the assertions: it is that the suite's answer depends on which runner invoked it and nothing anywhere says so.

title: perry-config write --from-file writes a zero-record store at exit 0 on a config.md with no settings, and every perry-task/perry-goals write is then refused forever while verify/diff/lint all report zero drift — the same command is both the cause and the only offered recovery (TASK-095 round 3, finding 2)
to: One command can put a project into a state only that same command is offered to repair, and it cannot. Run against a config file carrying no settings, `perry-config write --from-file` writes a zero-record store and exits 0; every subsequent task and goals write is then refused forever, while verify, diff and lint all report zero drift and so report nothing wrong.

title: tracks_source is on two published payloads (perry-state project.config, perry-diagnose work_modes) with four possible values and no entry in schema/ or reference/ — raised by two consecutive TASK-095 reviewers
to: `tracks_source` appears on two published payloads with four possible values and has no entry in the schema or in any reference page — so a consumer reading it has to guess what the values mean. Two consecutive reviewers raised it before it was filed.

title: test_host_support.TestOpenCodeDispatchLimit.test_concurrent_mixed_registers_do_not_exceed_global_cap is FLAKY under the parallel runner — red once on 2026-08-29 with an empty ~/.cache/perry/in-flight, green in isolation and green on two consecutive tests/run re-runs; same class as the already-filed queue-reconcile and scratchpad-baseline parallel races
to: A host-support test is flaky under the parallel runner: red once on 2026-08-29 with an empty in-flight cache, green in isolation and green on two consecutive re-runs. Same class as the queue-reconcile and scratchpad-baseline races already on the board — a concurrency defect that only appears under load.

title: duplicate ids: a duplicate on the BOARD silently deletes a stored risks/asks record on an ordinary write (risk_records/ask_records skip a seen id), and a duplicate IN THE STORE leaks one record's cleared onto the other and re-persists it — both predate TASK-203 and were unreachable before it
to: Duplicate ids destroy records silently, in two different directions. A duplicate on the BOARD deletes a stored risks or asks record on an ordinary write, because the record builders skip an id they have already seen; a duplicate IN THE STORE leaks one record's cleared state onto the other and then persists it. Both predate TASK-203 and neither was reachable before it.

title: a hand-REORDERED .perry/config.md § Tracks table is config-store-drift to perry-lint and silent to every other tool — defensible under principle A as written, but neither documented nor guarded; found by the TASK-095 round 6 V4 reviewer, who also notes records_out_of_stored_order and cells_wearing_decoration were each verified against only one fixture
to: Re-ordering the tracks table in `.perry/config.md` by hand reads as config-store drift to perry-lint and as nothing at all to every other tool. The behaviour is defensible under the principle as written, but it is neither documented nor guarded. The reviewer who found it also notes that two neighbouring behaviours were each verified against only one fixture.

title: after intake-sweep leaves the canonical intake store empty, perry-lint reports perry/intake.jsonl as NS-01 foreign state even though the intake contract says an empty file is still a store; recognize Perry's declared empty intake store without excusing a foreign same-name JSONL
to: After an intake sweep empties the canonical intake store, perry-lint reports `perry/intake.jsonl` as foreign state Perry did not write — even though the intake contract says an empty file is still a store. The fix has to recognise Perry's own declared empty store without also excusing a foreign file that happens to share the name.

title: Thin perry-state to a query over the six JSONL stores; the payload shape does not change
to: perry-state exists because `BOARD.md` was canonical and counting anything meant parsing a markdown table. With six JSONL stores the counting is a loop, so what is left worth keeping is the payload SHAPE it publishes, not its reader. DESIGN-014's user decision 1 was answered on 2026-09-01: thin it to a query over the stores rather than keeping or deleting it, and the published shape does not change.

title: The render must distinguish what is projected from what is canonical — TASK-199's scope on the surface ADR-010 creates
to: A render has to show which of the things it prints are canonical records and which are projections of them, or a reader cannot tell what is safe to edit. Blocked in practice on the two rows that create the render this property has to hold on. It replaces TASK-199, which carried the same scope and was dropped in error on 2026-09-01 in a way that could not be reversed.

title: DESIGN-015 F — P003-O3-KR2 is computed from the store and events, not asserted
to: The sixth row of DESIGN-015. It is what turns phase KR P003-O3-KR2 from a number somebody typed into a number something counted, by computing it from the linkage store and the event log. It should not be allowed to lag the rest of the sequence for that reason.

title: DESIGN-015 E — phase/<NNN>-linkage.md sheds its schema'd half
to: The fifth row of DESIGN-015: `phase/<NNN>-linkage.md` sheds the half of itself that is schema'd data once that data lives in the store. Separable and allowed to lag — unlike the add-time writer it does not gate P003-O3-KR2 — and it is DESIGN-013 hygiene rather than work serving that KR.

title: DESIGN-015 A — declare linkage.jsonl in claims[] and write its three record schemas
to: The first row of DESIGN-015's implementation plan, locked 2026-09-02: declare `linkage.jsonl` in Perry's claims list and write the three record schemas it will hold. Section 7 of that design carries the risk this creates — a new claimed path means a new namespace-collision warning in every existing Perry project.

title: DESIGN-015 B — import the 93 linkage records from phase/003-linkage.md into the store
to: The second row of DESIGN-015: import the linkage records that currently live in `phase/003-linkage.md` into the new store. The count filed with the row is a measurement rather than an estimate, so it is to be re-measured before importing and the difference reported if the register has moved.

title: DESIGN-015 C — move the six linkage readers to the store
to: The third row of DESIGN-015, and the one the whole sequence turns on: move the six linkage readers onto the store. It MUST land before the add-time writer, and the ordering is a hard constraint rather than a preference — a writer pointing at a store the readers have not moved to fails silently, with the edge landing while every reader still answers from the old document.

title: DESIGN-015 D — add --kr writes the edge, and the add event carries kr
to: The fourth row of DESIGN-015: `perry-task add --kr` writes the linkage edge itself and the add event carries it, which is what moves phase KR P003-O3-KR2 off zero. Blocked on the reader migration by the hard ordering constraint that row records. The design flags its own reading of user decision 3 as an interpretation, so if an explicit never-asked record was intended, this row changes with it.

title: a locked decision that gets no task row does not ship, and nothing links a design's plan step to the work that discharges it
to: Two directions of one missing edge, and this row is the design-to-task half: a locked design's plan step has no link to the work that discharges it, so a decision that gets no task row simply does not ship and nothing notices. Its sibling covers the task-to-design direction. Whoever picks either up should first decide whether one declared edge answers both, because two mechanisms for one relationship is how this project acquires a second translation table.

title: a locked design's implementation rows need not cite it, so a finished design reports as never handed off forever
to: The task-to-design half: an implementation row need not cite the design it implements, so a finished design can report as never handed off forever. The trap was measured as it fired — filing this row took DESIGN-001 from `impl_refs` 0 to 1 and emptied the pending list, with nothing implemented, because the counter is a literal text match. So the defect is two-sided: six real implementation rows count for nothing, and one row that merely says 'read DESIGN-001' counts as implementing it.

title: Measure the category split inside perry-task and perry-lint by call site, not by grep
to: Measure how bin/perry-task and bin/perry-lint split by CATEGORY, counted at the call site rather than by grep. It is the first step of DESIGN-014's implementation plan and the precondition for that document's central section being a measurement rather than an admission: the two files are 40% of bin/ and neither of them is one thing.

title: The writer can destroy the table it writes to, and perry-lint cannot see it
to: A writer can destroy the very table it is writing to, and perry-lint cannot see it happen. The row's SCOPE HAS DECAYED and must be re-derived before anyone starts: of the four hazards originally justifying it, two are now measurably false — the decisions index has no write site left, and the migration tool was deleted on 2026-08-31 — one needs confirming rather than inheriting, and one is doubtful. The underlying question may still be a real P0, but its population has to be re-measured before the work can be estimated.

title: Sweep bin/, viewer/ and tests/ for document handling that ADR-007 made dead
to: Sweep bin/, viewer/ and tests/ for document-handling code that ADR-007 made dead, and report what is dead against what is still load-bearing. Round 1 is the CENSUS only: the fence this row is eventually for is blocked on a product decision, and the phase says outright that the measurement is the input the user needs in order to answer it. The round does not fence anything and does not close the row.

title: perry-lint's _track_context reads the track register from .perry/config.md after the walk, so a store-only project gets no tracks rather than its own
to: perry-lint reads the track register out of `.perry/config.md` after resolving the project root, so on a project that keeps its config only in the store it returns no tracks rather than that project's own. It is strictly better than reading a FOREIGN register and it is still not reading `.perry/config.jsonl`. Reported by another row's agent rather than folded into that round, which is why it is a row instead of scope creep.

title: the Bound that review.md requires is never asked for where specs are written, so its absence costs rounds instead of minutes
to: review.md requires a bounded criterion and perry-lint reports its absence, but add-task — the only place a spec is ever written — never mentions `## Bound`. So specs are authored without one and the omission surfaces rounds later, which is a measured cost rather than a style preference: one row burned five review rounds, another eleven, and a census found the unbounded finding eight times across twelve review files.

title: nothing warns against writing a cross-reference to a row that has not been minted yet, and the id it guesses may land on the row doing the guessing
to: Nothing warns an author against writing a cross-reference to a task id that has not been minted yet, and the id guessed may land on the row doing the guessing. Observed when a row's next action said 'unlike TASK-280' predicting what the NEXT row would be numbered, and that row was itself minted as TASK-280, making the sentence self-referential. The existing rule forbids an example id that resolves to nothing; this one resolves, to the wrong row.

title: git-boundaries.md never says how to write a commit message, and Perry's own identifiers are backticked, so a -m string silently executes them
to: The git-boundaries page never says how to write a commit message, and Perry's documentation convention is backticked identifiers — so a `-m` string containing them has them executed by the shell and substituted away. It happened: a commit explaining the escalation gate's false positives named two fragments and shipped with both names simply gone. This bites Perry harder than most projects because nearly every honest commit message about its own code contains backticks.

title: perry-task's --actor is optional and defaults, so a write to a lane-owned file can have no owner any session can claim
to: perry-task's `--actor` is optional and defaults, so a write to a lane-owned file can end up with no owner any session can claim. The actionable core is that optional actor, NOT the incident that exposed it — five link edges were written that the session filing this could not account for, and the edges themselves turned out to be correct. The tool's own help already states the open question: DESIGN-004 asks whether actor should be mandatory and until that is answered an unset actor is recorded as unset.

title: the dispatch gate matches a path a spec CITES as if the spec wrote it, so an honest spec is refused and an incidental mention green-lights a real hit
to: The dispatch safety gate matches a path a spec merely CITES as though the spec were going to write it. Both directions are live and one is silent: honest specs are refused for naming the evidence file the round exists to produce, and one spec passed only because an incidental mention elsewhere cancelled a real hit, with no output distinguishing that from a genuinely clean scan. Same defect family as a design-id counter that cannot tell 'implements' from 'mentions' — a literal matcher standing in for intent.

title: close-task warns after the fact on a V4 whose verdict block cannot be parsed, so 10 of 27 V4 closures carry a rung nothing confirms
to: close-task lets a V4 closure through when its verdict block cannot be parsed, and perry-lint reports it only afterwards — so a rung can be claimed and merely questioned later, which is not a gate. Scoped to the FORWARD half: refuse the close. Whether the ten existing closures in that state should be re-reviewed or restated rewrites this project's own verification record and belongs to the user.

title: goals has no KR writer, so adding a KR means hand-editing okr.jsonl — build the writer
to: There is no write path for a KR record at all, so adding, restating or withdrawing one means hand-editing a file the documentation says is never edited by hand. It is now blocking a decided pivot: the user decided to withdraw a phase KR, the pivot procedure offers exactly that operation, and the tooling cannot perform it. The deliverable should cover both levels — the overall KRs in okr.jsonl and the phase KRs in the linkage file.

title: every NS-01 warning Perry emits is about a file Perry itself wrote, and the remedy each one offers is a no-op
to: Every namespace-collision warning Perry emits is about a file Perry itself wrote, and the remedy each one offers is a no-op — the warnings say 'move Perry's state to its own root' and the state root already IS that root. One of the five is a separate bug: a FILE claim whose warning tells the reader to move files out of a file. This is why every lint run reported warnings that every session skipped as pre-existing; a check that only ever cries wolf gets trained out of the reader.

title: the objective scanner's heading-depth test does not cover the claim its own docstring makes
to: A scanner's heading-depth test does not cover the claim its own docstring makes. Reported by a reviewer as a green mutation and correctly not charged as a failure — a green mutation is a finding either way, and here it is the second half of one: the guard does not test what it says it tests.

title: a store record's title field is unverifiable: planted garbage passes verify with drift 0 and byte_identical true
to: A store record's title field is unverifiable: plant garbage in it and `verify` still reports drift 0 and `byte_identical: true`. It matters because that sentence is what every store row in this project rests its acceptance on, and it is silent about any field the renderer does not read. Found while attacking a load-bearing claim and correctly ruled pre-existing rather than that row's defect.

title: a dispatched agent's pkill matches across the whole machine and killed another agent's suite
to: A dispatched agent's process cleanup matches across the whole machine and killed another agent's test suite. This is what concurrency looks like when the isolation is per-worktree but the process table is shared: the dispatch limit reserves slots and nothing scopes a signal. Worth pairing with the finding that the shared scratchpad is not private either — both are the same shape.

title: DESIGN-014's per-tool line counts drifted and were not re-measured at lock
to: DESIGN-014's per-tool line counts drifted and were not re-measured when the document was locked. Small on its own, but that document's whole method IS per-tool measurement, so a stale figure in it is the document failing its own standard rather than a typo.

title: bin/perry-config --help names perry-conform, a tool TASK-261 deleted
to: bin/perry-config's help text names a tool that was deleted. The argument that decides it came from the consumer who reported it: the guidance says to believe the contract table over the help text, but the help text is what a person actually runs — so Perry told a consumer to prefer one surface over another instead of fixing the one people invoke.

title: schema/README.md still tells a consumer to read the State root out of .perry/config.md, which is the render
to: schema/README.md tells a consumer to read the state root out of `.perry/config.md`, which is the projection rather than the register. Measured 2026-09-02, and the measurement makes the fix sharper than 'the page is stale': the tool resolves the state root itself and publishes it, including on a project that has no store, so a consumer that can run the tool never needs to parse the markdown and one that reads the store alone would get it wrong.

title: an evidence document produced a line count with an instrument that walks the filesystem, so it counted untracked bytecode
to: A line count in an evidence document was produced by an instrument that walks the filesystem rather than the git index, so untracked bytecode was counted into it. The lesson this row should carry is about instruments and about propagation: the wrong REASON for the wrong number had already been written into a locked design document, and correcting the board cell did not correct the artifact. A reviewer found it there and failed the round, correctly. A finding already written down somewhere needs the write chased, not just the record amended.

title: DESIGN-014's D-02 entry cites the branch by a moving ref, so its figure stops re-deriving the moment the branch advances
to: A design document's entry cites the branch it measured by a moving ref, so its figure stops re-deriving the moment that branch advances. Recorded by two consecutive reviewers and deliberately not charged by either, because it sits outside the round's bound and the review rules forbid widening one except by filing a row. This is that row. The item had already degraded further between the two rounds, which is the argument for it rather than against it.

title: green_lit does not de-duplicate across touches sections while refuse does
to: One half of a spec-scanning function de-duplicates across sections and the other half does not. Deferred in 2026-08 with a stated condition — the next change to that function — and the condition has now fired, so the deferral discharges into a row rather than expiring silently, which is the whole point of attaching a condition to one. Still cosmetic today: no spec repeats a fragment across two sections.

title: parsers.py:462 says the walk is skipped when handed an exact root, and the code walks four levels anyway
to: A parser's docstring says the walk is skipped when it is handed an exact root, and the code walks four levels anyway. CLOSING IT COSTS MORE THAN THE DOCSTRING GAP SUGGESTS and a correct fix will look like a regression unless it lands with its tripwire: the minimal fix turns another round's deliberate anti-vacuity test red, so whoever takes this must retire or invert that test in the same commit. Whether the minimal form is green suite-wide is unverified and should be established first.

title: three more fixtures carry a .perry/ with no events.jsonl, so the four-parent walk leaves them too
to: Three more test fixtures carry a `.perry/` directory with no event log, so the same parent walk escapes them too. Inert today for exactly one reason — none of the three ships a design directory — and adding a single design document to any of them re-opens the defect there with no warning and no test. Sequence it after the walk fix: if that makes the walk honour an explicit root, these three may need nothing at all.

title: 127 of 134 specs carry no ## Bound, and the check that would say so can only fire after the round it would have bounded
to: Almost every spec on this project — 127 of 134 — carries no `## Bound`, and the check that would report that cannot fire until after the round it would have bounded. The check is implemented and correct and it reports two, because it reads the criteria field OF A VERDICT BLOCK — so a spec is only reachable once a review has already been written against it. A post-hoc check on a pre-flight property. The two it does fire on belong to the row that failed two review rounds and hit the schema limit: it found the unboundedness by paying for it twice.

title: a dispatched agent's entire round lives in its context until one final commit, so any interruption costs all of it
to: Nothing a dispatched agent does reaches disk until its single terminal commit, so an interruption at any point before that costs the whole round. Measured on 2026-09-02: five agents were dispatched, the laptop was closed, all five died at the watchdog and git log across all five branches shows zero commits. Between fifteen and thirty minutes of work each, and the only surviving trace was the last sentence each had streamed. The cause was environmental, which is exactly why the row exists — an agent cannot prevent the interruption, but it can refuse to hold a round hostage to a single terminal commit.

title: two comments in tests/test_tree_guard.py assert evidence the round could not have measured and a set it did not enumerate
to: Two comments in a test file assert evidence the round could not have measured and a set it did not enumerate. One claims zero differences where 843 of 846 file modes differ; the other calls a file 'the only other file the copied run executes' where the enumeration finds twenty-four. Both are documentation defects against a round that passed on everything behavioural, and one edit closes both.

title: test_host_support.py admits four registrations through a gate whose global cap is three, and the runner calls it a flake without naming the mechanism
to: A host-support test admits four registrations through a gate whose global cap is three, and the runner's own docstring calls the module a known flake without naming the mechanism — which is the problem, because a named flake with an unnamed mechanism is indistinguishable from a real concurrency defect, and this one reads like one. Attributed rather than waved away: the module is red on a pristine archive of the base commit, one run in four under load.

title: test_tree_guard.py is now the suite's longest module at 48-124s, and its own fix is what put it there
to: This test module is now the suite's longest at 48-124 seconds, and its own fix is what put it there. It is NOT a regression and should not be read as one — the round that did it just passed review, and both of the things that cost the time are load-bearing. So the question is not whether the cost is justified but whether it is the right size. The 48-124 second spread is itself the first finding: the module's cost varies 2.6x with machine load.

title: the dispatch limiter has a race, found while three rounds ran concurrently
to: Perry's limiter for concurrent dispatches has a race in it, found while three review rounds were running at once. Reported by a round that deliberately left it outside its own bound, and filed here so the refusal discharges into a row rather than into a sentence in a result document. The limiter is the only thing coordinating concurrent agents on this machine, and five ran at once the night it was found.

title: a test-id fixture hard-codes the 3.11 id shape while its docstring says it was copied from a real run, and python3 here is 3.9.6
to: A test fixture hard-codes the test-id shape produced by Python 3.11 while its docstring claims it was copied line for line from a real run — and the interpreter this project actually runs is 3.9.6, where the ids collapse to the class name. Counts are unaffected, which is why it was not charged. The part worth knowing beyond this fixture is that two interpreters are in play here and they disagree about test identity.

title: a module red only from an unexpected success reports zero failed tests, the exact shape the fix argues against
to: A module made red only by an unexpected success reports zero failed tests — the exact zero-failures-under-a-red-module shape the fix that shipped argues against, arriving through the one door its guard does not cover.
